# TO THE KING.

SIRE,

It is said that the great, venerable, and Divine elder Hippocrates, father of Medicine <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) was an ancient Greek physician who is traditionally regarded as the "Father of Medicine."</note>, having—by a most particular gift from on high—predicted to the inhabitants of Greece the plague that was to come from the Illyrians <note>Illyria was an ancient region in the western Balkans; ancient texts often cited it as a source of pestilence.</note>; and shortly thereafter, by his Divine Art of Medicine, cured several inhabitants of that land of this pernicious disease. These people, in recognition of such a benefit, bestowed upon him great honors, which he dedicated to Hercules, as if recognizing this... <note>The author is drawing a parallel between Hippocrates’ honors and his own work, "The Chemical Hercules," suggesting that the strength to overcome disease comes from a "heroic" or divine source.</note>

Now, having received from the Eternal <note>A common 17th-century term for God.</note> the gift of healing those illnesses which are commonly held to be incurable, I come, SIRE, to hang this offering at the foot of your Altars; you who are the monster-chasing Hercules of Heresy, and the guardian God of the Church, and of the Elysium <note>original: "Elize," referring to France as a paradisiacal or "chosen" land.</note> of the eldest daughter of Europe, France. Under whose happy auspices I open and reveal the cavern <term>spelonque: an archaic term for a cave or grotto</term> that until now had held cheerful Health hidden away. And just as you have, by the divine fire of your Love, burned and consumed the Hydra of political factions and the Huguenot rebellion <note>This refers to the religious and civil conflicts in France; Louis XIII famously suppressed Protestant uprisings during this period.</note>, just as Hercules, the conqueror of monsters, burned and reduced to ashes the horrible serpent with regenerating heads; likewise, through the holy desire I have for the public health, I have endeavored to extinguish, suffocate, and reduce to nothing the regenerating Hydra of intractable diseases.

These [diseases], just as the body of that Serpent <note>Referring to the Hydra mentioned on the previous page, a multi-headed monster from Greek mythology.</note> disdainfully scorned the outrages of the sword and all that the force of iron <note>In this context, "iron" refers to both weapons of war and the surgical knives used by physicians.</note> can provide to men for the destruction of life: in the same way, they scorned both the medicines and the iron that until now the most skillful *Asclepiades* <note>Followers of Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine; the author uses this to refer to traditional, university-trained physicians.</note> have known how to apply. And just as all the forces of your predecessors were unable to suppress that daughter of Hell, Heresy, which you alone—great Hercules—have done, and that through the fire of your Love: in the same way, they have been unable by any means to overcome the Maladies that I treat in this work; namely Leprosy, Gout <term>Podagre: a historical term specifically for gout affecting the feet</term>, Dropsy <term>Hydropisie: an old term for edema, or the accumulation of excess fluid in the body</term>, Epilepsy, Cancer, "Touch-me-not" <note>original Latin: "Noli-me-tangere"; a term used by early modern doctors for corrosive skin ulcers or malignant growths on the face</note>, and Scrofula <term>Escrouëlles: also called the "King’s Evil," a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck</term>: for they were not Herculeses. But my Chemical Hercules, by a medicament made entirely of fire, drawn from Spagyrics <term>Spagerie: the alchemical practice of separating, purifying, and recombining the "essences" of natural substances to create potent remedies</term>, consumes this day all those Maladies which until now were held to be incurable.

<summary>The author argues that traditional medicine has failed to cure major diseases, just as previous kings failed to stop heresy, claiming his "Chemical Hercules" (spagyric medicine) provides the "fire" necessary for a cure.</summary>

# PREFACE.

One could rightly say that Surgical Medicine <term>Medecine Chirurgique: at this time, surgery and medicine were often treated as separate guilds; the author argues for their noble unification</term> is the most excellent, admirable, noble, and honorable science with which man can be provided in this world, if it were known according to its merits, received in its purity <note>original: "candeur," implying both sincerity and the untarnished state of the art</note>, and practiced with faithfulness. But insofar as we now see it more professed than faithfully cultivated, more labored over than advanced—the labor <note>original: "labeur"</note> in it being more in a circle than in progress, having much repetition and little addition—one can truly say that it has fallen from its glory and splendor. And it is not only fallen, but so changed, corrupted, and altered, that it is no more than an idol and a phantom: its face downcast <note>original: "aualée," meaning sunken or dejected</note>, its credit ruined, its honor degraded, its strength beaten down, and its reputation withered. In short, it has fallen from the highest rung of its greatness to which our predecessors had climbed and raised it. # PREFACE.

**Mathurin.** Yes, but perhaps they will cry out that novelty is greatly perilous in Medicine, and that all <term>Hermetic Medicine: A branch of medical practice based on alchemy and the "secrets of nature," named after the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus</term> being founded on new dogmas and on new remedies must be rejected. This they cannot say sanely without simultaneously renouncing—plainly and simply—the foundations of **Hippocrates**, and testifying falsely against his true dogmas: for if the dogmas of **Paracelsus** are new (as they say) and therefore must be rejected as they do, those of **Hippocrates** must be as well, insofar as **Paracelsus** constructs upon no other foundations than those of **Hippocrates**; building his Medicine only from the stones which **Hippocrates** himself used. 

This can be verified by examples drawn from both, which I have expressly brought to this place. For if one reads **Hippocrates** attentively in his *Book 1 of Diseases* when he says, *That everything in Nature is but one, and all things are but one thing*: he will find reading **Paracelsus** in his *Book of Torments* <note>original: "liure des Tourments." It seems to me that the parallels I draw in this place between these two doctrines should suffice for those most difficult to please, and for the greatest enemies of Paracelsus; for in these examples, one sees clearly how the one has said nothing that the other has not also alleged. If anyone wishes to hesitate further on this matter, let them know that disputes in Medicine are useless, just as Hippocrates says in the book *On Divination* <note>original: "de Diuinatione"</note>, Books 2 and 6.

### PREFACE.

...[I conduct myself] in such a way as to aspire no further than I can reach; but in that which is within the scope of my spirit, I shall not yield to those whose eyes are sunken and whose backs are bent with old age—here, I speak not of the weight of years, but of the weight of truth, reason, and experience. For in Medicine, the strongest reasons and the most certain experience are those that win the day.

The **Wise Babylonians** <note>The author refers to a famous account by the historian Herodotus, who claimed the Babylonians had no formal doctors but instead brought their sick to the public square so that anyone who had recovered from a similar illness could share their practical experience.</note> had no other Physician, nor any other preservative than experience: experience is the witness of success, the light of Medicine, the life of truth, and the capable mistress of the Arts. Likewise, all my studies, my sleepless nights, and my labors are found in my practice, my method, and my science: they are my conduct, my passport, and my letters of assurance. 

I pray the Reader not to hold in contempt the freedom of my Style, nor the unpolished words with which it is built; we are concerned here with curing diseases, which is achieved through the science and knowledge of the **mysteries of Nature** <term>mysteries of Nature: the hidden physical and chemical processes that early modern practitioners sought to uncover through experimentation.</term>, and not through eloquence. So too, I place my hope in God that the effects of my remedies and the healing of various diseases will reveal how great the **secrets of Nature** are, and show my experiments to be certain, for the benefit of the public and the satisfaction of individuals. 

For those who read this book attentively will experience and find, in fact, that my words have no other goal than the relief of the poor afflicted and the exaltation of God’s name. My profession invites me to this as a divine calling, summons me as a charitable duty, and drives me as a necessity above all others. Re- <note>This "Re-" is a "catchword," a common printing practice where the first syllable of the next page is printed at the bottom of the current one to ensure the pages are bound in the correct order.</note>

# THE BOOK
### TO THE READERS.

## STANZA.

Eminent minds in learning,
Fearing not to disappoint you,
Promise, before reading me,
That no manner of self-interest <note>original: *interest*, referring here to personal bias or ulterior motives that might cloud a reader's objectivity.</note>
Will cause you to pass judgment <term>judgment: the original French *arrest* refers to a formal or legalistic verdict, suggesting the author expects his work to be scrutinized as if in a court of ideas.</term>
Until the very end of my discourse:
Afterward, judge without passion <note>In the 17th century, "passion" often referred to emotional disturbances or prejudices that prevented clear, rational thought.</note>
Our good intentions.

### Extract of the Approval.

We, Charles de l’Orme, <note>Charles de l'Orme (1584–1678) was a highly influential French physician who served as the primary doctor to King Louis XIII and is famously credited with inventing the beaked protective suit worn by plague doctors.</note> Doctor of Medicine of the University of Montpellier, Counselor to the King, and Ordinary Physician to His Majesty, certify that we have seen the book titled *The Morbific Hydra Exterminated by the Chemical Hercules*, <note>original: "L’Hydre morbifique extermi-nee par l'Hercule Chimique." This metaphorical title suggests that disease—the multi-headed Hydra—can only be defeated by the strength of "Chemical" (alchemical) medicine, symbolized by Hercules.</note> which we have found does not make Chemistry a new form of Medicine, but rather, being full of the industrious preparation of remedies, it fortunately enriches the domain of Medicine. And we have judged it all the more useful because it strives to prove that, in essential matters, Paracelsus <note>A revolutionary 16th-century physician who championed the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> merely veiled the notions of the ancients under obscure and ambiguous terms; however, when these terms are well understood, they change neither the appearance nor the nature of things, but are found in the end to be in agreement with the principles and maxims of the science which, through reason and experience inseparably united, preserves the health of men and cures all curable diseases. Accordingly, we could not deny him our approval. Done at Paris, the 17th day of March, 1628. Signed, C. DE L’ORME.

<summary>This page concludes the alphabetical list of authorities cited in the book and provides a formal endorsement from the King's physician, Charles de l'Orme. The approval validates alchemical practices by arguing they are a sophisticated way to prepare remedies that actually align with ancient medical wisdom rather than contradicting it.</summary>

# Extract from the King’s Privilege.

By Letters Patent <note>A type of legal instrument or open letter issued by a monarch granting a right, monopoly, or status to an individual.</note> from the King, issued at Paris on the 3rd day of April 1628, signed **LOUIS**, and below, By the King, **DE LOMÉNIE**, etc., permission is granted to David de Planis Campy, Surgeon to His Majesty, to have printed a book he has composed titled *The Morbific Hydra Exterminated by the Chemical Hercules* <note>original: "L'Hydre Morbifique exterminee par l'Hercule Chimique." This allegorical title casts disease as the multi-headed Hydra of Greek myth, which can only be defeated by the "Chemical Hercules"—referring to the power of alchemical or spagyric medicine.</note>, etc., in such form, size, margin, and typefaces, and by such printer as he sees fit, for the duration and term of ten years, and to have it sold and distributed by such Bookseller or Booksellers as he chooses to select: With prohibitions to all Printers, Booksellers, and all others, of whatever status they may be, from printing or having printed the said book, both inside and outside the Kingdom, under color of any false mark, translation of language, change of title, or any other such disguise whatsoever; nor even to use the title or other material of the said book for any other work whatsoever, nor the figures and plates <note>Refers to the engraved illustrations included in the book.</note> found therein, without the consent of the said **DE PLANIS CAMPY**, upon penalty of one thousand livres in fines <note>A significant sum of money in 1628, intended as a serious deterrent against piracy.</note> payable to him, confiscation of all copies found to be counterfeit, and all costs, damages, and interests, notwithstanding any oppositions or appeals whatsoever, and all letters to the contrary, as is more fully contained in the said Letters Patent, by which His Majesty wills that by inserting an extract at the beginning or end of the said book, the original shall be considered well and duly notified to all those whom it may concern.

<header>The Morbific Hydra Exterminated</header>

<margin>Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> & the method he maintained there, and why.</margin>
taken in its true light; for Hippocrates and Paracelsus teach me to hold and maintain that there is no contradiction in their doctrine. The parallels I draw in this treatise between these two great figures will show that, until now, Paracelsus has been misrepresented. To this end, I provide the definitions of both, their causes, distinctions, signs, and prognoses; I explain their maxims <note>Original: "sentences," referring to the authoritative medical aphorisms or judgments of the ancients.</note>, untie their difficulties, and bring them onto the field to fight and strike down the monsters that until now have been held as inexterminable. I am driven to this for the honor of science, the profit and utility of students, and compassion for the sick—and not to attribute any glory to myself. Of which glory, if any spark returns to me, I consecrate and dedicate it from this moment to the Author of all wisdom. Let us then enter into the matter, and begin with the Galenic <note>Referring to Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), whose theories on the four humors dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> definition of Leprosy.

<margin>Definition of Leprosy according to Galen.</margin>
*Leprosy, according to Galen, is a very great illness, arising from an error in the digestive and blood-making power <note>The "sanguificative virtue" was the hypothetical power of the body to transform food into blood.</note> of the liver; by which error and defect, the assimilative power* <note>The "assimilative virtue" was the body's ability to take nutrients and turn them into the actual substance of organs and tissues. The text cuts off as it begins to describe how this failure leads to the disease.</note>

### *Admirable Precipitate of Mercury, according to our description.*

**Take:** Purified mercury, 4 ounces. Running mercury extracted from gold, 1 ounce. Put these two mercuries, mixed together, into a small long-necked **matrass** <note>a glass flask with a round body and a long neck used for heating liquids</note>, **luted** <note>sealed or coated with a protective layer of clay or paste to withstand heat</note> all around. One must continue the fire until the whole is precipitated into a **red powder** <note>likely red mercuric oxide, a substance historically used in medicine despite its high toxicity</note>. Once rectified, this is a most sovereign purgative against **Leprosy**, as well as against all malignant and foul-smelling ulcers, **Cancer**, **Touch-me-not** <note>original: "Noli-metangere"; a historical term for corrosive skin ulcers, often referring to basal cell carcinoma</note>, and **Scrofula** <note>original: "Escroüelles"; a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck</note>. It loosens the bowels very gently, and can be given without danger to women and small children. It purges the **phlegm** <note>original: "pituite"; one of the four bodily humors believed to cause sluggishness or respiratory issues</note> and tempers the hot and dry disposition of the [bodily] parts. The dose is from six **grains** <note>a traditional unit of weight based on a single grain of cereal, roughly 65 milligrams</note> to ten. One can also make this **Precipitate** with common mercury **amalgamated** <note>combined or alloyed</note> with gold leaf, but it does not possess as great a virtue as the one described above.

Now, **Paracelsus** marks this 24 in this way: 2. 4. 0., which **Dariot** <note>Claude Dariot (1533–1594) was a French physician who became a prominent advocate and translator of Paracelsus’s medical theories.</note> has explained incorrectly as twice 24, making 48, multiplied by five: for five times 48 makes two hundred and forty. ### CHAP. I.

<margin>Definition of Dropsy according to Hippocrates.</margin>
All the Hippocratics <note>Followers of the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates, representing the traditional school of medical thought based on the four humors.</note> aim for the same goal regarding the definition of Dropsy <note>original: "Hydropisie"; known today as edema, it is the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities.</note>, which they say is, *a tumor against nature, watery,*

--- Page 263 ---
<meta>This page continues the definition of Dropsy (edema) from the Hippocratic perspective before introducing the specific alchemical definition provided by Paracelsus. The author seeks to reconcile traditional humoral medicine with the newer chemical medicine of his time.</meta>

*The Morbific Hydra Exterminated* <note>The title of the work, appearing here as a running header at the top of the page.</note> made of an abundance of Water, windiness, or phlegm <note>original: "pituite"; in the humoral system, this was the cold, moist humor associated with mucus and respiratory secretions.</note> gathered sometimes in the whole habit of the body, other times in some part: but most often in the cavity of the lower belly; generated from the error or weakness of the digestive power <note>original: "vertu digestive"; the innate biological force believed to govern the transformation of food into bodily substance.</note> of the liver, or of the spleen. ### ->C H A P. III.<-

### CHAP. V.

<margin>At what times Epileptic paroxysms are most intense.</margin>
Epileptic **paroxysms** <note>The peak or most violent stage of a seizure.</note> are much more intense when the **Moon** begins to be full, or when it is new, than at any other time, or even when it occupies the Heart or the Brain; for then the **humors** <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> are in excess; especially when, after the North Wind, the South Winds blow; winds which, just as they are certainly tempestuous and unhealthy, are also cold and humid. Now this disease, as **Hippocrates** <note>An ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) regarded as the father of Western medicine.</note> maintains, arises from a cold and humid cause and matter: as it appears, because he says that they are cured by the change of weather, seasons, and locations. In this context, it refers to the "temperament" or the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within the body.</note> of the body warmer and drier. ->*Quintessence of Human Skull.*<-

Take filings of a human skull that has not been buried <note>Early modern medicine often specified "unburied" skulls—such as those from soldiers or the gallows—believing they retained the "vital spirits" that would otherwise be lost to the earth.</note>. ->*White Amber Oil, wonderful against Epilepsy.*<-

->*Anti-epileptic Laudanum.*<-

<term>Take</term> <note>original: "Pr."; an abbreviation for the Latin "recipe," the standard opening for a medical prescription.</note> red sandalwood powder, 1 ounce; yellow sandalwood powder, 1 ounce; powders of mace, galangal, black and long pepper, aloeswood, and cinnamon, 3 ounces <note>original: "ana ℥ .iij."; "ana" is a Greek-derived term meaning "of each."</note> of each; make an extract with spirit of wine <note>original: "esprit de vin"; high-proof alcohol used as a solvent.</note>. ### Anti-epileptic of Paracelsus.

<margin>Paracelsus, volume 3, page 374.</margin>
<term>Take</term> <note>original: "Pr."; the Latin abbreviation for "recipe."</note> Roman or Hungarian <term>Vitriol</term> <note>original: "Vitriol Romain, ou d'Hongrie"; metallic sulfates, often used in early chemistry to produce acids.</note>, 15 pounds; peony liquor, camphor, ivory shavings, and <term>spodium</term> <note>original: "spodij"; often referring to bone ash or metallic oxides produced by fire.</note>, half an ounce of each. Afterward, take 3 pounds of this liquor; rectified spirit of wine, lemon balm water, and valerian water, half a pound of each; and 1 pound of <term>colcothar</term> <note>original: "colcotar"; the red iron oxide residue left after distilling vitriol.</note>. Distill through the <term>cornute</term> <note>original: "cornuë"; another term for a retort.</note> for a full day and night, and there will emerge the <term>phlegm</term>, <term>spirit</term>, and <term>oil</term> <note>In early chemistry, these represent the three fractions of distillation: the watery part, the volatile medicinal part, and the heavy concentrated part.</note>. Then, separate the phlegm using a <term>Bain-marie</term> <note>original: "Bain Marie"; a gentle water bath.</note>, the liquor (spirit) using an ash bath, and the oil using a sand bath with a strong fire. The phlegm is for children: the dose is 1 <term>drachm</term> <note>original: "ʒ j."; approximately 3.9 grams.</note> before the <term>paroxysm</term> <note>original: "paroxisme"; a sudden attack or seizure.</note>. The liquor is for older individuals, in a dose of 1 <term>scruple</term> <note>original: "℈ j."; approximately 1.3 grams.</note>. The oil is for those over 40 years old: the dose is three drops, taken with celandine or marjoram water.

<header>The Morbific Hydra Exterminated <note>original: "l'Hydre Morbifiq. exterminée"; likely the title or section of the treatise, referring to the "Hydra" of diseases being destroyed by the "Hercules" of chemistry.</note></header>

[Take] <note>The OCR "nez" is likely the end of "Prenez" (Take).</note> the <term>dregs</term> <note>original: "fæces"; the solid residue remaining after a substance has been processed</note>, grind them, and place them in a long-necked <term>flask</term> <note>original: "matras"; a chemical vessel used for digestion and distillation</note>; over them, pour its own water that you previously drew off, so that the liquid rises three fingers above the solids. ### Method for Preparing the Salt, or Emetic of Vitriol, called the Vomiting Manna of Vitriol <note>original Latin: "Manna vomitoria vitrioli." Manna refers to a crystalline or sweet substance; here it is used for a purified chemical salt.</note>.

<margin>Manner of calcining the vitriol.</margin>
Take Hungarian <term>vitriol</term> <note>a metallic sulfate mineral, in this case likely copper sulfate, used in early medicine and chemistry</note>, which should be the color of an <term>azure stone</term> <note>original: "pierre d'azur"; referring to lapis lazuli</note>. Have it <term>calcined</term> <note>heated to a high temperature to drive off moisture and impurities</note> in a sufficiently large crucible, using a strong <term>wheel fire</term> <note>original: "feu de roüe"; a furnace arrangement where charcoal or fire surrounds the vessel to provide even, intense heat</note>, until it turns into a powder of a violet or dark purple color; then it is well calcined. However, if it does not have this aforementioned color after being calcined, but is only red like <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>original: "bol Armene"; a reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent</note>, even if you think you will draw a beautiful white Salt from it, you will only obtain vitriol of the same color, form, and taste as it was before. 

<margin>Observations.</margin>
Also, if it is over-calcined until it becomes black, spongy, and light, and too deprived of its <term>acid spirit</term> <note>original: "esprit acide"; the volatile acidic vapors (sulfuric acid) released during heating</note>, it will yield very little Salt, and what it does yield will have no purgative effect at all, or very little.

These aforementioned things being duly observed in the calcination of vitriol, you will extract the Salt in this manner.

Take a large glass vessel, into which you will put a good quantity...

<margin>Virtues of the Salt of vitriol.</margin>
This Salt purges the stomach of superfluities and <term>corrupt humors</term> <note>in the medical theory of the time, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that caused disease when out of balance</note> adhering to it, without any danger. ## CHAP. VII.
### *Oil of sublimed Mercury.*

<margin>Definition of the Touch-me-not, according to the Galenists.</margin> *The Touch-me-not is a cancerous ulcer of the face, creeping and horrific, accompanied by a biting corrosion, burning, and stinging, with a foul virulence and wicked rot.*

### Regarding the treatment of the *Noli-me-tangere*.

## C H A P T E R  VI.

<margin>Guy de Chauliac, chapter 2, doctrine 2, treatise 4.</margin>
The treatment of the *Noli-me-tangere* <note>Latin for "touch me not"; a historical name for a corrosive facial ulcer, often what we now call lupus vulgaris or a rodent ulcer</note>, according to Guy de Chauliac <note>A famous 14th-century French physician and surgeon</note>, should be similar to that of a canker <note>a spreading or malignant sore</note>; prescribing that after general management—which concerns the lifestyle of the patient—and the evacuation of the underlying cause—whether by purging or bloodletting—and the preservation and strengthening of the internal organs, it will be necessary to focus on the specific treatment. This will involve the use of oxycrate <note>a mixture of water and vinegar</note> with aluminous water <note>water containing alum, used for its astringent and drying properties</note>, and afterwards an ointment made with the juice of plantain <note>a common healing herb</note>, toadflax <note>linaria</note>, and rock salt. These are cooling and drying remedies, which should be applied around the area (to soothe the stinging sensation) using cloths soaked in the juice of cold herbs. And later, if these remedies are of no use, he refers the Surgeon to cauteries <note>burning the tissue with heat</note> and corrosives <note>harsh chemicals used to eat away diseased flesh</note>, while recommending prudence due to the delicacy and sensitivity of the face. To carry out this method—

### CHAP. VII.

*Sweet Oil of Mercury.*

Take two parts spirit of nitre <note>Nitric acid</note> and one part well-purified Sal Ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride; used here with nitric acid to create "aqua regia," a solvent capable of dissolving noble metals.</note>. Distill these together using a retort <term>retort: A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</term>. Then afterward, take whatever quantity of mercury sublimate <note>Mercuric chloride, a highly toxic and corrosive salt of mercury.</note> you wish; pour this liquid over it until it floats two or three fingers deep. Digest this in a closed vessel, then distill it. Pour the liquid back over the residue (which must be ground up beforehand), repeating this operation as many times as necessary until the sublimate remains fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixing" a substance means making it non-volatile so it no longer evaporates or changes state when heated.</note> at the bottom.

## *Aqua Vitae of Saturn.* <note>original: "Eau de vie de Saturne." In alchemy, Saturn is the symbolic name for lead. "Aqua Vitae" (water of life) refers here to a potent distilled essence or spirit.</note>

Take 15 ounces <note>The symbol ℥ represents an ounce; xv is the Roman numeral for 15.</note> of lead white <term>lead white (ceruse): a white pigment made of lead carbonate, used historically in both paints and cosmetics</term>; pulverize it and pour boiling distilled vinegar over it, stirring vigorously with a stick, and in no time at all, the vinegar will become charged with the dissolution of the lead white. Pour off the clear liquid and repeat with fresh vinegar, continuing until all the lead white is dissolved. Evaporate the vinegar (which will be as tasteless as water) until the Salt remains congealed at the bottom. <note>This "Salt" is lead acetate, often called "Sugar of Lead" because of its sweet taste, though it is highly poisonous.</note> Have a sufficient quantity of this, and place it in a retort <term>retort (cornuë): a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances</term> that is half full; place it on the furnace with an open base <note>This indicates placing the vessel in direct contact with the heat source rather than using a sand or water bath.</note>, driving off with a gentle fire at the start whatever foreign moisture might have remained there. And when white fumes begin to appear, attach a sufficiently large receiver <term>receiver (recipiant): a vessel used to collect the condensed product of distillation</term> and seal the joints well with lute <term>lute (luter): an airtight paste or cement used to seal the connections of laboratory glassware</term>; then, gradually increasing the fire until it becomes very strong and the retort is buried in the coals, you will see emerging like a small tor- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "torrent."</note>

<margin>Observation for the perfection of the oil of wax.</margin>
Alternatively, in order to give this oil the scent and color of wax, you must take 2 parts of new wax and one part of the aforementioned oil of wax. Reduce the wax into small pieces which you will mix with the oil, then distil the whole through a retort <term>retort: a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-curving neck, used for distillation.</term> over ashes with a slow fire; separate the oil from the water using a funnel and keep it for use.

<margin>Virtues of the aforementioned oil.</margin>
This oil resolves <term>resolves: in a historical medical sense, to dissolve, disperse, or "thicken" a swelling or morbid humor.</term>, attenuates, penetrates, softens, and dissipates, by rubbing the affected part after having mixed it with an equal amount of oil of scorpions <note>original: "huile de scorpions." A traditional alchemical remedy made by infusing scorpions in oil; it was believed to have potent warming and analgesic properties.</note> and oil of bricks <note>original: "huile de briques." Also known as *Oleum Lateritium*, this oil was produced by quenching hot bricks in oil and then distilling the result; it was used for treating joint pain and stiffness.</note>.

Oil of turpentine <term>turpentine: a volatile oil distilled from pine resin, frequently used in early medicine for its "drawing" and warming qualities.</term> is also admirable for softening and dissipating, but since everyone knows the method for making it, I will refrain from describing it for the sake of brevity; furthermore, it can be found in full perfection in our *Spagyric Pharmacopoeia* <note>original: "Pharmacopee Spagerique." This refers to a medical text based on spagyric (alchemical) principles of "separating and recombining" to purify medicinal substances.</note>; in place of which oil, we shall describe here an admirable resolutive.

### *Resolutive Oil for Scrofula.*

Take: half a pound of oil of bricks <note>original: "huile de briques." Also known as *Oleum Lateritium*, this was prepared by soaking hot bricks in oil and distilling them; it was prized for its ability to "resolve" or dissolve hard swellings.</note>; frankincense, mastic, gum arabic, and turpentine, 3 drachms <term>drachm: an apothecary unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</term> of each. Mix everything together and distill using a retort <term>retort: a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-curving neck, used for distilling liquids.</term>; add to this liquid the essential salt of vipers <note>essential salt of vipers: a substance extracted from the flesh of vipers, believed in early modern medicine to be a potent "volatile salt" capable of purifying the blood and curing skin diseases.</note> and keep it for use. This oil powerfully softens and resolves <term>resolves: to disperse or dissipate a swelling or "morbid humor."</term> scrofula <term>scrofula: a tuberculous infection of the lymph nodes in the neck, historically called the "King's Evil."</term> by anointing them two or three times a day.

---

### *Plaster of Sulfur.*

Take: 3 ounces of balm of sulfur; 3 drachms of colophony <term>colophony: a solid, translucent resin obtained from pines; also known as rosin.</term>; 1 and a half ounces of wax; and as much myrrh as the total weight of the other ingredients. Melt the wax and colophony together with the balm, mixing in little by little the finely powdered myrrh; cook the whole over a slow fire, stirring constantly with a spatula for a quarter of an hour. Form it into magdaleons <term>magdaleons: cylindrical rolls or sticks of medicinal plaster that could be sliced and softened for application.</term> and keep for use. This is for all kinds of tumors, wounds, and ulcers, applying it morning and evening; it encourages suppuration <term>suppuration: the process of forming or discharging pus, often viewed historically as a way for the body to expel "corrupt" matter.</term>, breaks, cleanses <note>original: "mondifie." To "mondify" a wound meant to clean it of dead tissue or impurities to allow for healing.</note>, and heals within a few days.

<margin>All things are produced from the 4 Elements, and by what means.</margin>
<margin>It is man’s nature to learn.</margin>

Whereupon I beseech you, Dear Reader, to give thanks with me to this good heavenly Father, God, Author & Creator of all things, who by his ineffable <term>ineffable|Something so great or sacred that it cannot be expressed in words.</term> goodness & incomprehensible mercy, has distributed to the things here below so much virtue for the sole consideration of man, his creature: & furthermore has given the knowledge of them to wise Physicians, in order to put them into use for our benefit. Far removed from the Holy Spirit are those who not only despise them, but who hate them even unto death, for it is he who teaches us through the mouth of the wise man not to despise the Physician, nor the medicines he has created.

Thus it is that we are exhorted by the spirit of God not to despise the Physician, nor the remedies for which it has pleased Him, in His mercy, to grant us knowledge. For it is true that when one organizes the experiences and observations noted in the cure of diseases, it is God who permits and wills it so. Those who despise those who practice Medicine in all faithfulness are therefore far removed from all virtue. But enemies of God are those who not only despise Physicians, but who also heap slanders upon them. Truly, it must be confessed that such people are more worthy of pity than of hatred; of pardon and mercy than of punishment; of good counsel than of confusion—though it is nonetheless necessary to answer the fool according to his folly, so that he does not believe himself to be wise. <note>This is a reference to the biblical proverb (Proverbs 26:5): "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit."</note> Nevertheless, I pray to God from the depths of my soul that He might deign to grant them a ray of His holy grace, and through the power and efficacy of His Holy Spirit, withdraw them from the very bitter gall <note>The "bitter gall" is a common biblical metaphor for a state of sin or spiritual blindness.</note>

<summary>The author concludes a biblical citation from Sirach 38 and argues that disdaining doctors and their remedies is an affront to God, who provides medical knowledge through nature and observation.</summary>

<keywords>Physician, divine mercy, medical ethics, experimental observation, slander, Holy Spirit, biblical defense of medicine</keywords>

### *Errors occurred during printing.*

Page 19, line 13, read: of a dog. l. 14, read: is. p. 58, l. 7, read: spirits. p. 62, l. 23, read: fixed. p. 147, l. 19, read: congealed. p. 157, last line, read: Arthritic. p. 158, l. 10, read: book 1 <note>original Latin: "lib. i."</note>. p. 180, l. 21, read: seem. p. 181, l. 1, read: effects <note>original Latin: "effectus"</note>. p. 88, l. 22, read: Jejunum <note>original Latin: "Ieiunum," referring to the middle section of the small intestine.</note>. p. 210, l. 1, read: <term>Spagyria</term> <note>Spagyria refers to Paracelsian alchemy, specifically the process of separating and recombining the essential components of plants and minerals to create medicine.</note>. p. 220, l. 1, read: <term>ana</term> <note>A medical term derived from the Greek, used in recipes to mean "of each" or "an equal amount of each."</note>, which was omitted. p. 252, l. 12, read: to put, which was omitted. p. 280, l. 12, read: how many species there are. p. 284, l. 24, read: received. p. 290, l. 27, read: serum. p. 296, l. 17, read: made. p. 304, last line, read: amber. p. 310, last line, read: corrosive. p. 347, l. 13, read: they attach. p. 351, l. 20, read: it attaches. p. 398, l. 9, read: adding. p. 431, l. 15, read: reiterate. l. 17, read: you will withdraw. p. 491, l. 15, read: singular. p. 496, l. 8, read: must. p. 517, l. 14, read: skill. p. 545, l. 2, read: the water will separate from it.

Besides these small errors, one might perhaps encounter some faults in the punctuation, as well as some imperfection in the spelling; all of which arose from the little leisure I had for proofreading, which gave way to the negligence of the Printer.

<summary>This final page provides a religious closing to the treatise and an extensive list of errata (printing corrections) for the entire 576-page volume. The author concludes by asking for the readers' prayers and blaming punctuation errors on his own lack of time and the printer's haste.</summary>
